chunks.text: 2 Methodology 2.1 Problem Formulation Let I I denote a WSI and Y Y its corresponding slide-level label. First, I I is divided into a bag of N N patches 𝒳 = { x i } i = 1 N \mathcal{X}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} , where each patch x i x_{i} represents a tissue region cropped from the WSI. Then, a feature extractor F ​ ( ⋅ ) \texttt{F}(\cdot) transforms each patch into an embedding space, yielding the set of patch embeddings ℋ = F ​ ( 𝒳 ) = { h i } i = 1 N \mathcal{H}=\texttt{F}(\mathcal{X)}=\{h_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} where h i ∈ ℝ D h h_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\text{h}}} and D h D_{h} is its dimension. An MIL module MIL ​ ( ⋅ ) \texttt{MIL}(\cdot) aggregates ℋ \mathcal{H} into a slide-level embedding e = MIL ​ ( ℋ ) ∈ ℝ D h e=\texttt{MIL}(\mathcal{H})\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\text{h}}} , which is used to produce the slide label. In practice, N N can be very large, and many patches may be redundant or non-informative. Motivated by recent works on MIL that pinpoint the uneven distribution of patches, our objective is to construct an efficient and effective TTIS framework that identifies a compact, informative subset at inference time: ℋ ′ = TTIS ​ ( ℋ ) such that ℋ ′ ⊂ ℋ , | ℋ ′ | = M ≪ N \mathcal{H}^{\prime}=\texttt{TTIS}(\mathcal{H})\quad\text{such that}\quad\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{H},\quad|\mathcal{H}^{\prime}|=M\ll N (1) where M M is the subset size. We then compute e ′ = MIL ​ ( ℋ ′ ) ∈ ℝ D h e^{\prime}=\texttt{MIL}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime})\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\text{h}}} , that maintains or even improves the slide-level prediction compared to using the exhaustive set ℋ \mathcal{H} . 2.2 Test-Time Instance Selection Framework TTIS operates in three steps: (1) hierarchical spatio-semantic clustering to partition patches into groups capturing both spatial organization and morphological similarity, (2) stratified deterministic sampling to select representative patches while maximizing diversity, and (3) ensemble aggregation across multiple sampling configurations to improve and stabilize predictions. 2.3 Hierarchical Spatio-Semantic Clustering TTIS employs a hierarchical clustering strategy to partition the patch embeddings ℋ \mathcal{H} into groups that preserve both spatial coverage and semantic diversity. It utilizes a two-stage K-Means++ [ 1 ] clustering, which provides robust centroid initialization and faster convergence compared to standard K-Means . Specifically, we first cluster patches based on their 2D spatial coordinates into K 1 K_{1} clusters, capturing broad spatial organization. Within each spatial cluster, patches are further sub-clustered based on their feature embeddings into K 2 K_{2} sub-clusters, representing local semantic heterogeneity [ 2 ] . This hierarchical process yields a total of K 1 × K 2 K_{1}\times K_{2} sub-clusters. To ensure balanced granularity at both hierarchical levels, we set K 1 = K 2 = K K_{1}=K_{2}=K , resulting in K 2 K^{2} sub-clusters in total. 2.4 Stratified Sampling Given the sub-clusters, TTIS conducts stratified sampling to select a compact yet diverse set of representative patches. We adopt Farthest Point Sampling ( FPS ) [ 7 ] as the core sampling method and use diverse initialization strategies to enhance representativeness. Farthest Point Sampling FPS is a greedy downsampling algorithm widely applied in 3D point cloud analysis [ 17 , 22 ] . For each sub-cluster 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , FPS constructs a subset 𝒬 ⊂ 𝒮 \mathcal{Q}\subset\mathcal{S} by iteratively selecting the patch that is farthest from the current selected set.

Formally, at iteration t t with current set 𝒬 t − 1 \mathcal{Q}_{t-1} , the next patch is chosen as: q t = arg ​ max s ∈ 𝒮 ∖ 𝒬 t − 1 ⁡ min q ∈ 𝒬 t − 1 ​ ‖ h s − h q ‖ 2 . q_{t}=\argmax_{s\in\mathcal{S}\setminus\mathcal{Q}_{t-1}}\ \min_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{t-1}}||h_{s}-h_{q}||_{2}. (2) This procedure typically starts from an initial patch q 1 q_{1} , which is chosen randomly or by a deterministic rule, and repeats the above step until the target subset size is reached. This encourages broad coverage of the sub-cluster 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , while preventing over-representation of densely clustered regions. Starting Point Selection FPS is highly sensitive to starting point selection, which can yield inconsistent subsets across runs. To ensure deterministic behavior and enhance subset representativeness, we explore three deterministic initialization criteria. First, centroid-based initialization selects the patch closest to each sub-cluster centroid 𝐜 \mathbf{c} as the FPS starting point: s ctr = arg ​ min s ∈ 𝒮 ⁡ ∥ h s − 𝐜 ∥ 2 s_{\text{ctr}}=\argmin_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\lVert h_{s}-\mathbf{c}\rVert_{2} . Second, attention-based initialization leverages attention scores generated by attention-based MIL models [ 9 , 15 , 18 ] . Within each sub-cluster 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , we select the patch with the highest attention score as the FPS starting point: s attn = arg ​ max s ∈ 𝒮 ⁡ a s s_{\text{attn}}=\argmax_{s\in\mathcal{S}}a_{s} ,where a s {a_{s}} denotes the attention score assigned to patch s s . For MIL models that do not output explicit attention scores, we derive pseudo-attention scores using softmax-normalized L 2 L_{2} norms of the patch embeddings: a s = exp ⁡ ( ∥ h s ∥ 2 ) ∑ j ∈ 𝒮 exp ⁡ ( ∥ h j ∥ 2 ) a_{s}=\frac{\exp(\lVert h_{s}\rVert_{2})}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\exp(\lVert h_{j}\rVert_{2})} .

Third, class-guided initialization employs a pretrained pathology foundation model (e.g., TITAN [ 5 ] and MUSK [ 24 ] ) to identify the most diagnostically relevant patch as the starting point for each class. Given C C task-specific diagnostic categories, we define K K text prompts for each class following the standard practice of [ 14 ] . A text encoder produces prompt embeddings ℰ = { e k ( c ) ∣ c ∈ { 1 , … , C } , k ∈ { 1 , … , K } } \mathcal{E}=\{e_{k}^{(c)}\mid c\in\{1,\ldots,C\},k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\} . Averaging prompt embeddings per class yields the class prototype embeddings ℰ ¯ = { e ¯ ( c ) } c = 1 C \bar{\mathcal{E}}=\{\bar{e}^{(c)}\}_{c=1}^{C} where e ¯ ( c ) ∈ ℝ D t \bar{e}^{(c)}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\text{t}}} and D t D_{\text{t}} is the prompt text dimension. For each patch s ∈ 𝒮 s\in\mathcal{S} , we calculate the cosine similarity between its embedding h s h_{s} and each class prototype embedding: sim s ( c ) = h s ⋅ e ¯ ( c ) ∥ h s ∥ 2 ⋅ ∥ e ¯ ( c ) ∥ 2 . \text{sim}_{s}^{(c)}=\frac{h_{s}\cdot\bar{e}^{(c)}}{\lVert h_{s}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert\bar{e}^{(c)}\rVert_{2}}. (3) The patch with the highest similarity to each class c c becomes the class-specific starting point: s cls ( c ) = arg ​ max s ∈ 𝒮 ⁡ sim s ( c ) s_{\text{cls}}^{(c)}=\argmax_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\text{sim}_{s}^{(c)} . This yields C C class-specific starting points per sub-cluster for FPS . 2.5 Multi-view Test-time Ensemble Each initialization criterion emphasizes a unique facet of tissue representations, spanning semantic representativeness (centroid), model-specific importance (attention), and diagnostic specificity (class-guided). Relying on a single criterion may discard complementary information. To maximize robustness and predictive consistency, we propose a multi-view test-time ensemble that produces a slide-level embedding for each criteria and aggregates these embeddings using softmax-normalized weights.

The aggregated embedding is then fed into the classifier to produce the final slide-level prediction. 3 Experiments 3.1 Datasets We evaluate TTIS on five publicly available datasets. We use CAMELYON16 dataset [ 6 ] , comprising 399 WSIs, for binary tumor vs. non-tumor classification, and four TCGA datasets [ 21 ] for cancer subtyping: (1) Breast (TCGA-BRCA), containing 875 WSIs of invasive ductal and invasive lobular carcinoma, (2) Esophagus (TCGA-ESCA), containing 954 WSIs of adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, (3) Kidney (TCGA-RCC), containing 905 WSIs of papillary, chromophobe, and clear cell carcinoma, and (4) Lung (TCGA-NSCLC), containing 167 WSIs of adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. 3.2 Implementation We integrate TTIS with six MIL models: ABMIL [ 9 ] , TransMIL [ 18 ] , CLAM-SB [ 15 ] , WiKG [ 11 ] , S4MIL [ 8 ] , and R 2 T-MIL [ 20 ] . All WSIs are processed at 20 × 20\times magnification using non-overlapping 256 × 256 256\times 256 -pixel patches. Patch features are extracted using UNI [ 3 ] , and the MUSK [ 24 ] text encoder is employed for class-guided starting point initialization. We set the sampling ratio to r = 30 % r=30\% . For clustering, K-Means++ centroid initialization is performed 10 times, and the number of clusters K K is set to 16 for all datasets except TCGA-ESCA, where K = 2 K=2 due to smaller average patch counts per WSI. To ensure validity, all experiments are conducted with 3-fold cross-validation under a fixed random seed and implemented on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. We use CAMELYON16 dataset [ 6 ] , comprising 399 WSIs, for binary tumor vs. non-tumor classification, and four TCGA datasets [ 21 ] for cancer subtyping: (1) Breast (TCGA-BRCA), containing 875 WSIs of invasive ductal and invasive lobular carcinoma, (2) Esophagus (TCGA-ESCA), containing 954 WSIs of adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, (3) Kidney (TCGA-RCC), containing 905 WSIs of papillary, chromophobe, and clear cell carcinoma, and (4) Lung (TCGA-NSCLC), containing 167 WSIs of adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. 4 Results 4.1 Main Results Table 1 reports the classification and subtyping performance of the six MIL models under three conditions: (1) baseline (no instance selection), (2) with random sampling, and (3) with TTIS . Overall, TTIS consistently improves or preserves performance relative to baseline (processing all patches). On CAMELYON16, TTIS demonstrated substantial improvements over both baselines and random sampling. Compared to baselines, it achieved the best accuracy and F1 score in all models with gains of 0.52%-3.62% and 0.005-0.041, respectively.

Random sampling consistently underperformed both baselines and TTIS , indicating that naive instance selection degrades performance. Moreover, similar trends were observed across the four TCGA cohorts. TTIS generally matched or improved baseline performance across the six MIL models. On TCGA-BRCA, TTIS outperformed baselines with respect to accuracy and F1 score in 5 out of 6 models, yielding notable improvements in accuracy by up to 2.09% (ABMIL) and F1-score by up to 0.036 (WiKG). On TCGA-ESCA, TTIS yielded consistent gains for ABMIL and TransMIL in all evaluation metrics (e.g., 2.40% and 1.19% in accuracy and 0.025 and 0.012 in F1 score), and improvements in accuracy and F1 score for CLAM-SB, S4MIL, and R 2 T-MIL, while maintaining competitive AUC. On TCGA-RCC and TCGA-NSCLC, TTIS largely preserved baseline performance, with modest gains for several models (e.g., TransMIL/S4MIL on TCGA-RCC and CLAM-SB/WiKG on TCGA-NSCLC) with negligible differences in AUC. Specifically, on TCGA-RCC, it matched or increased accuracy in 4 out of 6 models (e.g., TransMIL from 95.00% to 95.77% and S4MIL from 92.31% to 93.08%), and on TCGA-NSCLC, it matched or exceeded baseline accuracy across all six models, highlighted by a 1.50% gain for WiKG. In these cohorts, overall performance differences between baseline, random sampling, and TTIS were minimal. These marginal improvements are likely attributable to inherent performance saturation, as evidenced by CLAM-SB on TCGA-RCC and ABMIL on TCGA-NSCLC, where all three experimental conditions obtained identical performance. Table 2 shows the results of ablation experiments on these three components using ABMIL, which frequently obtained the best overall performance among the six MIL models. For instance selection and ensemble, we analyzed the individual performance of each initialization method. Each individual initialization method generally improved performance compared to the baseline (i.e., no instance selection), with the exception of TCGA-RCC. Notably, the proposed multi-view test-time ensemble, combining all three initialization methods, matched or provided modest improvements over any single method, indicating that the different strategies capture complementary sets of instances, and their integration provides more robust WSI representations. To investigate the effectiveness of hierarchical clustering, we varied K ∈ { 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 } K\in\{2,4,8,16\} and compared them against a baseline that does not conduct clustering ( K = 0 K=0 ). Except for TCGA-RCC, hierarchical clustering provided consistent improvements over the baseline and remained remarkably stable with varying values of K K . This indicates that TTIS is highly robust to the specific choice of cluster count, and hierarchical clustering captures spatial and semantic heterogeneity. To understand the trade-off between efficiency and accuracy, we varied the sampling ratio r r from 100% to 10%. Overall, TTIS exhibited remarkable robustness under substantial downsampling. Notably, TTIS with r < r< 100% often outperformed the baseline, demonstrating that processing all patches is sub-optimal. These findings empirically validate the core premise of TTIS : WSIs contain substantial quantities of redundant and uninformative patches. Removing these redundant and non-diagnostic patches at inference suppresses noise that would otherwise confound the MIL aggregation, thereby improving overall predictive performance.

Removing these redundant and non-diagnostic patches at inference suppresses noise that would otherwise confound the MIL aggregation, thereby improving overall predictive performance. 5 Conclusion We propose TTIS , a training-free, plug-and-play test-time instance selection framework for WSI analysis. Since TTIS requires no retraining or architecture modifications to pre-trained MIL models, it guarantees seamless integration into existing computational pathology pipelines. By employing hierarchical spatio-semantic clustering followed by FPS , TTIS constructs a compact yet representative patch subset directly at inference time. To further improve robustness, TTIS employs a multi-view ensemble strategy that combines patch subsets derived from complementary initialization criteria: centroid-based, attention-based, and class-guided, each capturing a distinct facet of tissue representation. Extensive experiments across five public datasets demonstrate that TTIS consistently improves or matches the performance of baseline MIL models.
